newsitem.title: FRANCE: French right faces possible rout in Paris.
newsitem.headline: French right faces possible rout in Paris.

text.p: France's ruling centre-right faces a possible rout in Paris, one of its traditional strongholds, where 10 of its 19 deputies face strong challenges in next Sunday's parliamentary election run-off.

Among the government elite in danger of losing their National Assembly seats are the capital's mayor Jean Tiberi, Justice Minister Jacques Toubon, Environment Minister Corinne Lepage, Employment Minister Anne-Marie Couderc and Patrick Stefanini, a senior aide to Prime Minister Alain Juppe.
All but Lepage are members of the Gaullist Rally for the Republic (RPR), the party of Juppe and Jacques Chirac who was mayor of the city until he was elected president two years ago.

The looming leftist breakthrough in the parliamentary poll follows a similar development in June 1995 mayoral elections, when Socialists won five of the capital's 20 municipal districts and ended a longtime Gaullist lock on the city government.

Paris results in the first round of the snap parliamentary election were in line with a national shift towards the leftist opposition But they stood out because of the right's longtime dominance in the capital, where it held 19 of 22 districts in the outgoing assembly.

The strong vote against government candidates is also an embarrassment in his own city for Chirac, who dissolved the assembly nearly 10 months early in order to seek a friendly parliament for the final five years of his seven-year term.

Instead, Chirac now faces the possiblity of a period of power-sharing with a leftist government, which he has warned could tie France's hands in the international arena and derail his drive to modernise its economy and bring it into European monetary union.

Tiberi, Chirac's longtime ally and the target of a sleaze probe, led Socialist rival Lyne Cohen-Solal by just five percentage points and experts predicted the second-round vote would be extremely close.
The weak showing reflected voter anger at the mayor over sleaze scandals in the capital. Twenty-eight people ran against him in his Left Bank district.
Tiberi, a member of parliament since 1968, is under judicial investigation over alleged payment of a fictitious salary to his wife Xaviere by a Gaullist-run local authority in the Paris region.

Tiberi also was president of the Paris housing authority at a time when mayor Chirac's RPR allegedly received illicit funding through kickbacks on public housing contracts, according to another judicial probe.

In another wrinkle in the Tiberi race, Ecology Generation candidate Bernard Raquin alleged that his ballots were missing from voting stations, and he planned to ask the constitutional council to cancel the first-round election in his constituency.
Toubon, who is also mayor of the capital's 13th district, was in a tight runoff with Socialist opponent Serge Blisko, whom he led by about five percentage points.
Rightist candidates, including Gaullist ex-prime minister Edouard Balladur, appeared in better shape in nine other Paris constituencies, analysts said.
